opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a word that makes people nervous, and I think for good reason, because "planning" can sound like we're attributing some rich, deliberate, human-style intention to the model. So I try to be pretty concrete about what I mean by it.

The naive picture of a language model is that it's just predicting the next token, one at a time, with no sense of where it's going. And mechanically, that's true: it does output one token at a time. But what we've found when we look inside these models is that the computation producing a given token can already represent things that are going to come several tokens later. That's the sense in which I'd call it planning.

The example I like is rhyming poetry. If you ask a model to write a couplet, and the first line ends with a word like "grab it," a naive next-token story would say the model just writes the second line word by word and then, at the very end, scrambles to find something that rhymes. But when you look at the internal features, you see that right at the start of the second line, before it's written any of it, the model is already representing candidate rhyming words, something like "rabbit." Then the rest of the line gets constructed to land on that word. And you can intervene on it causally: if you suppress the "rabbit" representation or swap in a different target word, the model writes a different line that ends on the new word. So it isn't just correlation; that internal representation is actually steering what comes out.

So when I say planning, I mean something fairly specific: the model represents a future goal or target internally, and that representation shapes the intermediate steps it takes to get there. It's working backward from a destination, not just forward from the last token.

What I'd be careful about is overgeneralizing. Finding this in a poem doesn't mean the model has some general-purpose long-horizon planning module that it uses everywhere, or that it plans the way a person does. It's more that "it's just predicting the next token" turns out to be a pretty misleading description of the internals, even though it's accurate about the interface. The interesting work is figuring out how far ahead this kind of lookahead goes, in which tasks it shows up, and how reliable it is.

r001.rationale: The response separates the label “planning” from human-like intention and grounds it in a specific internal process: representing a future target that shapes intermediate steps.

r002.rationale: It says the model represents candidate rhyming words at the start of the second line, before those words appear several tokens later.

r003.rationale: It explains that the rest of the line is constructed to land on the candidate word and describes this as working backward from a destination.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think "planning" is one of those words that people get a little nervous about, because it sounds like we're attributing something very human to the model. And I want to be careful here, because the way I think about it is almost purely mechanistic. When we say the model is planning, what we actually mean is something very specific: at a given point in the computation, we can find features inside the model that represent a token or a concept that it isn't going to output for several more tokens, and those features are causally influencing what it does right now.

The cleanest example we found is in poetry. If you give the model a couplet, something like "He saw a carrot and had to grab it," and you look at what's happening at the newline before the second line, you'd naively expect the model to just be thinking about the next word. It's a next-token predictor, after all. But instead you see features firing for words like "rabbit" or "habit," candidate rhymes for the end of the line. And then the model writes a line that steers toward one of those words. If you go in and suppress the "rabbit" feature, or inject "green" instead, the whole line reorganizes around the new target. So the end of the line is being decided, in some representational sense, before the beginning of the line is written.

To me that's the honest definition of planning here. It's not that the model has an intention in some rich sense, or that it's deliberating. It's that it's representing a future outcome and then working backwards from it. And I think that's actually a really interesting thing to find, because the training objective never asked for it. Nobody said "please pick your rhyme first." It just turns out that if you want to be good at predicting the next token in a poem, it's useful to have already settled on where the line is going. So planning falls out of prediction.

I'd also say we should be a bit humble about what we can and can't see. We're looking at these snapshots through tools that are imperfect, so when I say the model is planning, I mean we've found evidence of this forward-looking representation in specific cases and shown it matters causally. I wouldn't want to generalize that into "the model has a plan for the whole essay" without actually going and checking.

r001.rationale: It frames “planning” as a specific, causally influential internal representation of future outcomes, while distinguishing that mechanism from humanlike intention or deliberation.

r002.rationale: It describes rhyme candidates such as “rabbit” appearing at the newline before the line is written, with those words intended for the line’s end several tokens later.

r003.rationale: It says the model steers the line toward a represented rhyme and that the line reorganizes around an injected future target, describing structure formed around that word.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish two things. One is the task the model is trained on, which is predicting the next token. The other is what it might need to do internally to get good at that task. Predicting the next token doesn’t necessarily mean you’re only reasoning about the next token. If you’re generating a solution to a problem, it can be useful to anticipate where that solution is going.

But I’d be careful about taking a coherent answer as evidence that the model planned the whole thing in advance. It could be following patterns it learned, or doing some computation that looks more like planning. Those can produce similar-looking outputs.

Then there’s planning at the system level, where you explicitly have a model propose a sequence of actions, take an action, observe the result, and revise its plan. That’s a more concrete sense in which we can talk about planning, because we can examine whether it anticipates consequences and adapts when something doesn’t work. That’s different from saying we know how it’s organizing the answer internally.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes observable planning-like behavior and system-level planning from claiming that the model internally planned its answer.

r002.rationale: It does not state that model circuitry generates candidate words many words ahead of their eventual position.

r003.rationale: It does not describe working backward from a candidate future word to determine sentence structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by planning. A language model is trained to predict the next token, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us what computation it learns to do to make that prediction. To predict what happens next in a complicated situation, it can be useful to represent where things are going and some of the steps needed to get there.

But I’d distinguish that from saying every response involves a plan. If a model produces a convincing sequence of steps, that alone doesn’t establish that it considered alternatives or checked whether those steps would work. The interesting question is behavioral: can it work toward a goal, anticipate consequences, and revise its approach when something changes? That’s where I’d look for evidence of planning.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes outward behavior—producing steps or working toward a goal—from what computation the model internally uses, and says convincing steps alone do not establish internal planning.

r002.rationale: It does not say the model’s circuitry generates candidate words many words ahead of their eventual position.

r003.rationale: It does not describe working backward from a candidate future word to determine sentence structure.
